title: Earn-In Equity for Journeymen Buying Trade Shops
one_liner: A platform that turns a retiring HVAC, plumbing or electrical owner and a 25-year-old journeyman into a multi-year vesting buyout with a pre-agreed valuation formula, seller note and SBA-ready paperwork.
customer: Retiring owners of 5-40 employee trade shops (sellers pay) and licensed journeymen or foremen aged 22-35 (buyers), plus SBA lenders that fund the final tranche.
problem: Most trade-business owners plan to retire within years, yet only about half have a succession plan. Selling to private-equity roll-ups strips the local shop, and employees cannot get $1M+ loans with personal guarantees or clear the licensing hurdles. Owners hesitate to leave, and buyers lack a track record that lenders trust.
solution: An 'earn-in': the journeyman converts part of pay, bonus and sweat into equity tranches at a formula price (a multiple of trailing owner earnings with a collar), while the owner keeps a seller note and consulting role. The platform supplies valuation, legal documents, state-by-state license-qualifier planning, a data room from job and dispatch software, and a lender packet. After three to five years it supports the final SBA-financed buyout, monitoring callbacks and margins as an early-warning system.
why_now: An estimated 6 million small-business ownership transitions and up to $5T of enterprise value are expected by 2035, and Gen Z interest in trades and acquisition is rising. Lenders want buyers with operating history, which a staged earn-in builds. Field-service software now produces clean data to underwrite from.
revenue_model: A seller-paid setup fee of $4-$8k, a 1% fee on closed value plus lender referral, and a SaaS charge of $99-$299 per month for tracking tranches and KPIs. Later, a small gap-capital fund.
non_obvious_insight: The successor is already inside the business, and the bottleneck is trust and time, not capital. A formula-based earn-in makes 'when and at what price' knowable on day one, lets owners retire on a schedule, and lets buyers learn to run the shop before taking on debt. It also preserves local reputation better than a roll-up.
first_30_days: Recruit five retiring owners through local supply houses and trade associations. Charge $2,500 for a pilot 'succession blueprint' plus legal docs. Interview 20 journeymen through trade schools and union halls. Partner with an M&A attorney and one SBA lender. Aim for three signed earn-ins by month six.

title: Shared-Docket Lawsuits Against Scam Infrastructure
one_liner: Turn Google's and Microsoft's civil-seizure playbook into a membership where 20-50 mid-size banks and brands co-file one John Doe action against the kit or ring impersonating all of them.
customer: Regional banks, credit unions, toll and payment operators, and mid-market retail and logistics brands that are repeatedly impersonated. They are too small to fund a $1M lawsuit alone.
problem: Takedown notices are whack-a-mole. Criminal enforcement takes years, and the FBI is warning about $1.6B+ in law-enforcement impersonation alone. Phishing kits sell for about $50, and one E-ZPass smishing ring sent 330,000 texts a day and took about $1B over 3 years. Big Tech gets ex parte orders to seize domains and servers, but mid-size victims are left with abuse reports.
solution: An evidence-and-litigation-ops company paired with an independent law firm (fees billed separately, to respect fee-splitting rules). It continuously builds dossiers on the kits hitting its members and drafts one multi-plaintiff John Doe complaint (Lanham Act, CFAA, RICO where apt). It then obtains TRO and preliminary-injunction orders that compel registrars, registries, hosts, CDNs, and stablecoin issuers to act. Members pay a retainer plus a per-seizure fee and receive the takedown results.
why_now: Google's 2025 suit against the operators of the Lighthouse smishing kit and Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit seizures created templates and precedents. Kits are centralized, so one order can protect hundreds of brands. The US-UK agreement to coordinate scam-center takedowns (Sep 4 2026) signals political tailwind for civil action.
revenue_model: $2-5K per month per member. 30 members is roughly $1M ARR. Success fees per seized infrastructure cluster. Legal costs passed through.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation cost scales with the number of defendant networks, not the number of victims, so it works like a reverse class action: fixed cost, split N ways. Kit concentration means a single order hits infrastructure serving hundreds of brands. Everyone assumes only Microsoft and Google can afford this, and nobody sells it as a shared product.
first_30_days: Retain a boutique IP/cyber litigation firm. Recruit 5 founding members through a credit-union league or toll-operator association. Deliver each an evidence dossier on the kit currently hitting them. Pre-sell $2K/month founding memberships to fund the first filing within about 90 days.

title: Shared-Aide Pods for 55+ Apartment Buildings
one_liner: One on-site aide team serves 6-10 residents in the same building, delivering assisted-living-style help at a fraction of 1:1 home-care cost.
customer: Owners and operators of independent-living and 55+ apartment buildings (market-rate, senior LIHTC and HUD-202 properties). The payers are middle-income residents and their families, who can't afford $75-130k a year and are stuck on waitlists.
problem: Home care is sold as one aide per client per hour ($35 an hour, about $80k a year for 44 hours a week) only because of legacy billing. Assisted living is at 90% occupancy with almost no new supply before 2030. Residents who age past independent living either move out or go without.
solution: A licensed home-care agency subsidiary (or partnership with one) posts 2-3 aides per shift inside the building. They run scheduled 15-45 minute ADL, medication-reminder, meal-setup and toileting visits, plus overnight response. Dispatch software handles acuity tiers and in-building routing (floors, elevators). Residents buy monthly tiers of about $1,800-3,500, and the property gets a retention amenity.
why_now: NIC MAP shows 57 of 99 metros above 90% occupancy, units under construction at a 2012 low, and no meaningful new supply before 2030. Medicaid HCBS is walled off by 15-month waitlists and labor is scarcer after the 2026 visa pause, so stretching each aide across more clients is the only lever left.
revenue_model: Monthly resident subscription by care tier, with a revenue share or amenity fee to the property owner. Later, Medicaid HCBS or managed-care billing for pods in affordable senior buildings.
non_obvious_insight: Aide hours are cheap to make dense (no drive time, no client-hour minimums) but are priced as if they were mobile. The gap between 1:1 pricing and 1:8 cost is the whole business, and only a property-anchored operator can capture it. Assisted-living-without-the-license is a real category nobody has scaled.
first_30_days: Sign a 90-day pilot with one 100-200 unit 55+ property in a tight market. Subcontract to an existing licensed agency to move quickly, staff a two-aide pod, and target 15 residents at about $2,200 a month. Track aide minutes per resident and move-out avoidance.

title: Independent Leakage Audits for Age Verification
one_liner: A red-team lab that measures how easily under-16s slip past each platform's age check (VPN, borrowed ID, face tricks) and sells defensible evidence to platforms, counsel and insurers.
customer: Mid-size social, gaming and video platforms operating in Australia, the UK, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and US ban states. Also their outside counsel and, later, regulators.
problem: Insiders treat age assurance as a vendor-selection problem. Regulators judge whether 'reasonable steps' were taken. Australia is investigating five major platforms (fines up to A$49.5M) and proposed in June 2026 to double fines to about A$99M and reach app stores and age-assurance providers. By February 2026 many children had already bypassed the ban. Vendors self-report accuracy but nobody independently measures real-world leakage at the 14-17 border.
solution: A standard test harness of about 20 evasion scenarios (VPN region switch, parent's ID, older-sibling account, face-estimation edge cases, re-registration). It runs with consented adult testers and synthetic profiles, never with minors. Outputs are a quarterly public 'Leakage Index' plus confidential 'reasonable-steps evidence packs' and a continuous monitoring subscription.
why_now: Bans went live between December 2025 and June 2026 and enforcement is starting. The proposed extension of liability to age-assurance providers means everyone in the chain wants third-party evidence. The reported IDScan breach and Persona complaints (both from the brief, one flagged shaky) push platforms to question their vendors.
revenue_model: Confidential audits at $15-60k each. Monitoring subscription at $3-10k a month. Later, licensing the test protocol to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: This is an assurance market like SOC 2, not a technology market. The buyer wants a defensible paper trail, and it must be independent of the vendors it grades, so the lab should be paid by the platforms rather than the vendors.
first_30_days: Write the 20-scenario protocol with a regulatory lawyer. Run it on 5 public age gates in Australia using adult test accounts, keeping to what counsel clears. Publish a free 'Leakage Index' teaser. Cold-email trust-and-safety leads and regulatory counsel at 40 mid-size platforms with their own results.

title: Verified-Offer Shield Against H-2A Recruitment Scams
one_liner: A WhatsApp-native registry where growers publish verifiable H-2A job offers and authorized recruiters, so workers can check any offer in seconds and growers get proof they never sanctioned a fee-charging middleman.
customer: Grower associations and large H-2A employers, plus farm labor contractors running H-2A programs, who pay per worker. Workers use it free.
problem: H-2A is scaling as the domestic workforce shrinks (over 300K visas in 2024; EPI expects growth toward 500K jobs after the Oct 2025 wage rule; the workforce reportedly fell by at least 155,000). Fake recruiters and impersonated grower pages sell nonexistent jobs or charge illegal fees. H-2A rules make employers contractually responsible for banning recruiter fees, so a scam in a grower's name is a compliance and reputation hit. Late or absent arrivals mean unharvested crops.
solution: Growers verify their business identity once, attach a DOL job-order number and issue a signed offer card with a QR and short code. Recruiters receive a 'licensed by grower' credential. A worker-side WhatsApp and SMS bot works in Spanish and through voice notes for Indigenous-language speakers (Mixtec, K'iche'). It replies 'verified', 'not found' or 'fee reported' and takes fee complaints. Growers get an audit trail of their recruiter chain and arrival tracking.
why_now: The immigration crackdown removed workers, and strawberry and almond growers reportedly lost up to 30% of crews in early 2026. The H-2A wage rule changed the incentives. AI makes fake job pages, voices and documents cheap. WhatsApp Business APIs are mature, and nobody in agriculture has a verification layer.
revenue_model: $15-40 per worker per season paid by the employer or association, a premium tier for recruiter-chain audit trails and DOL-ready records, and possible lender or insurer sponsorship.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the grower, not the victim. Growers carry the legal and commercial exposure to recruiter fraud and have the budget, while workers cannot pay. Verification for the poor is funded by the party with compliance liability.
first_30_days: Sign one grower association for a pilot with 3 member farms. Build the WhatsApp bot on the Meta Cloud API. Recruit 2-3 recruiter partners in Mexico and Guatemala. Collect 20 real scam examples through worker centers and legal-aid groups, and use them to demonstrate detection.

title: Walker Brain: Clip-On Sensor for Rollators
one_liner: A $60 clip-on pod that turns any walker or rollator into a fall alarm, night-light and gait-speed monitor, so there is no wearable to forget.
customer: Home-care agencies and PACE programs (buying for clients), DME suppliers, Medicare Advantage and ACO care teams, and adult children buying directly.
problem: Pendant alarms fail because many seniors won't wear them or press them. People who use walkers are among the highest fall-risk group, yet smart-walker work is mostly academic prototypes. Gait speed predicts decline and hospitalization but is measured in a clinic once a year, if at all.
solution: A clamp-on pod with an IMU, LTE-M connectivity, a small LED light strip, tip and fall detection and grip sensing. It detects when the walker is actually being used versus left by the bed at night, which is itself a leading risk signal. It auto-alerts on tipping and sends a weekly gait report and decline flags to family and the care team. Battery lasts months and the senior needs no app.
why_now: Low-power LTE-M and IMU chips are cheap. Medicare Advantage plans are measured on fall-risk management, and home-care agencies are looking for differentiation. The DME channel has not changed in decades, and the walker sensor category is still mostly prototypes.
revenue_model: Hardware $59-79, family subscription $8-12/month. B2B: about $6 per pod per month for agencies, or a per-member-per-month fee for plan pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Don't ask an 80-year-old to adopt a new device. Instrument the one object they can't give up and that is with them exactly when risk peaks. 'Walker left behind at night' is a signal no wearable can capture.
first_30_days: Prototype with off-the-shelf LTE-M dev boards and a 3D-printed clamp. Place 30 pods on walkers with 3 home-care agencies as free trials. Measure alerts and gait trends. Aim to convert 2 agencies to 100-unit pilots, and talk to outpatient physical therapists about a small validation study.

title: Chip-to-Billet Solid-State Metal Mini-Mills
one_liner: Turn aluminum machining chips directly into billet, rod or wire by friction extrusion, with no remelting, first as a tolling service and then as on-site micro-mills.
customer: Aerospace, defense and precision machine shops with segregated 6061 and 7075 chips, plus extruders and AM wire makers who want recycled content.
problem: Machining chips sell for a fraction of ingot value and are remelted with real melt loss and energy. Aerospace buy-to-fly waste is huge, and domestic aluminum is exposed to tariffs and supply shocks.
solution: Solid-state processing (friction or shear-assisted extrusion, developed at national labs) consolidates single-alloy chips into bar or wire feedstock, preserving alloy chemistry. Phase 1 is a tolling service: ship chips in, get billet back. Phase 2 is a leased on-site mini-mill.
why_now: Tariffs on imported aluminum rose to 50% in mid-2025 and defense and aerospace capacity is stretched. Solid-state processes moved from lab demos toward pilots, so a first product now exists.
revenue_model: Tolling fee per pound returned, then equipment lease plus per-pound fee, plus recycled-content premiums.
non_obvious_insight: Melting destroys the metallurgical history. Chips from a single-alloy shop are effectively pre-alloyed, so solid-state consolidation captures value that a remelt discards.
first_30_days: Partner with a national lab or press builder. Run sample consolidations on chips from 3 shops and test tensile properties. Sell pilot lots to 2 extruders. Apply for AFWERX or SBIR support.

title: IEEPA Refund Ledger for CPAs and Controllers
one_liner: An accounting workbench that turns IEEPA refund data into correct inventory, cost-of-goods, tax and audit entries.
customer: CPA and advisory firms serving importers, and controllers at $10M-$500M manufacturers and distributors.
problem: About 330,000 importers paid about $166B on 53M entries. CBP had repaid about $86.3B by 2026-07-10, and AD/CVD and liquidated-entry cases come later. Each refund must be split between duty still in inventory, duty already in cost of goods sold, and interest, each with different book and tax treatment (UNICAP, state conformity, LIFO layers). CFOs have no playbook and brokers do not touch accounting.
solution: Import ACE entry-summary exports and broker data. Match each entry line to inventory layers or sales. Compute period-by-period reversal entries. Produce journal entries, a tax memo, a state schedule and a reconciliation to CBP statements. Model cash-tax timing for Q4 estimates. Export to QuickBooks, NetSuite and Sage.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with year-end close and Q4 estimated payments (due 2026-12-15 for calendar-year C corporations) approaching.
revenue_model: $750-3k per client engagement through CPA firms. $15-40k a year for white-label licenses. It grows into a standing duty sub-ledger for Section 232 changes.
non_obvious_insight: A refund is an accounting event, not a customs event. Every refund creates an inventory-basis and tax problem the broker will not touch, and the same ledger becomes the duty sub-ledger firms need as Section 232 rates keep changing.
first_30_days: Approach 10 CPA firms with importer clients. Build an Excel and Python prototype on three real entry datasets. Sell the first engagements at about $1.5k. Have a tax partner review the methodology.

title: Recertified Used Transformer Exchange
one_liner: A test-and-warranty marketplace that turns utility-retired transformers into energizable supply for data centers, solar and storage projects, instead of scrap.
customer: Data-center developers, solar and BESS EPCs, rural co-ops and industrial plants (buyers), sourcing from utility surplus desks and scrap dealers.
problem: AI data centers, solar, storage and grid upgrades have stretched transformer lead times to years, and tariffs on imported electrical steel and equipment make it worse. Meanwhile serviceable retired units are sold to scrap dealers priced by weight, worth a small fraction of a working unit.
solution: Buy or consign retired pad-mount and small substation units, run a standard test protocol (turns ratio, winding resistance, insulation, oil dissolved-gas analysis, PCB screening), refurbish through partner shops, and warrant them for 1-3 years. Units that fail go to core (grain-oriented steel) and copper recovery.
why_now: Transformer scarcity is the 2025-26 gating item for energization across data centers and solar/BESS. Tariffs on steel and derivatives raise new-unit prices, and developers are now willing to pay for schedule certainty.
revenue_model: 10-20% margin or commission ($3-15K per unit), plus $2-5K test and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: Scrap yards price transformers by weight, while buyers price them by lead time. The arbitrage is a test-and-warranty product, not hardware. The trust layer includes PCB screening, which incumbents avoid.
first_30_days: Sign 3 scrap dealers or utility surplus contacts and contract a test lab. List 20 units with spec sheets. Approach 5 solar and BESS EPCs with schedule pain and close 2 paid pilots.

title: Surety Bonds for Agent Operators
one_liner: A customs bond for bots: agent operators post a surety-backed bond so sites, APIs and merchants can say yes to their agents and get paid if the agents misbehave.
customer: Mid-size vendors of browser, shopping and procurement agents ($1M-$50M ARR) whose agents get blocked or throttled. They pay for the bond and credential. Merchants and API providers consume the signal for free.
problem: Agent identity schemes (signed agents, know-your-agent) say who an agent is, not who pays when it scrapes abusively, mis-buys or triggers chargebacks. Agents are cheap to recreate, so identity carries no cost of failure. Bots are now 57.4% of requests, so sites default to blocking. After the August 2026 Ninth Circuit Comet ruling, blocking has to rest on contract and technical measures, so sites need a concrete reason to let agents in.
solution: Underwrite the operator (KYB, behavior review, volume caps). Issue a surety or insurer-backed bond ($25k-$1M penal sum) plus a signed credential that plugs into existing agent-auth headers and protocols. Sites whitelist a bonded lane with higher rate limits. A small claims desk pays on signed request logs. Wedge: agent vendors selling into mid-market merchants and B2B API providers that would create a bonded lane in their bot rules.
why_now: Bots overtook humans in 2026, and the Ninth Circuit ruling shifts blocking to contract terms. Neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding agent-dispute rule, and Visa's merchant dispute threshold tightened to 1.5% in April 2026, so merchants are risk-averse. Bonding has been proposed only in academic papers so far, and no product exists.
revenue_model: Bond premium share (typically 1-3% of penal sum per year) plus a $500-$5,000/month underwriting and credential fee, plus surety agency commission.
non_obvious_insight: Trust that scales in commerce rests on bonds, not identity. Freight brokers, contractors and customs brokers all post bonds. A bond makes an operator's reputation costly to abandon, and a site only has to trust the surety, not the operator.
first_30_days: Partner with a small surety agency or MGA to draft a miscellaneous bond form and a claims evidence standard. Recruit 5 agent vendors that merchants block and 5 merchants or API providers willing to whitelist. Sell the first 3 pilot bonds at $500-$1,500 per year plus a setup fee.

title: Buffet Lab: Hotel Breakfast Lines as Test Market
one_liner: Paid two-week trials that put reformulated or novel ingredients on real hotel and cruise breakfast lines, with item-level consumption, waste and hot-hold colour data.
customer: Food manufacturers facing the FDA petroleum-dye phase-out, and makers of natural colours and alternative proteins such as fermentation whey, rubisco and purple-sweet-potato colour, including farmer-owned processors. Hotels and cruise operators are the supply side.
problem: Dye reformulation costs $50K-$500K per SKU and takes 12-24+ months, and Walmart private label goes dye-free in January 2027. Whey is short and alt-protein funding has collapsed, so startups need cheap real-world proof. Lab sensory panels and retail test markets are slow, expensive and blind to failure modes like colour fade under lights, texture after hot-hold, and portion rejection by the roughly 12% of Americans on GLP-1s.
solution: Recruit 30-50 independent hotels plus one cruise or resort operator. Supply product free and track item-level consumption against control, plate waste, restock rates by daypart, QR feedback, hot-hold time and light exposure, with colorimeter photos of colour drift. Optionally A/B half-portions. Deliver a two-week acceptance, waste and stability report, and sell recurring access to the panel to CPG innovation teams.
why_now: The FDA dye phase-out targets December 2027, with 22 states adding food-restriction rules and a federal ultra-processed food definition in review. Whey concentrate is up 108% in two years, alt-protein funding fell to $881M in 2025 with only $197M in H1 2026, and GLP-1 users are reshaping portions and protein preferences. Buyers want supply-risk answers, not sustainability stories.
revenue_model: $12K-$30K per product trial. Hotels receive product, about $40/day and waste analytics. Panel subscriptions for CPG innovation teams of $60K-$120K/yr.
non_obvious_insight: A hotel breakfast line is the largest measurable eating experiment in commerce: repeat business travellers, captive choice, fixed hot-hold time and lighting, and a natural weigh-back at clearing. It stress-tests exactly the things that kill natural-colour and protein reformulations, much faster than a retail test market.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 independent hotels via an owners' association and approach 5 natural-colour and ingredient startups directly. Run one paid pilot, for example a dye-free pastry glaze or cereal, at about $8K to prove the report format.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.

title: Cash Advances Against Steam Payouts
one_liner: A receivables-and-ad-float lender for live Steam games, underwritten from the studio's own Steamworks wishlist and sales data instead of the game's quality.
customer: Steam-live indie studios and micro-publishers with roughly $50k-$1M a year in net Steam revenue and 100+ reviews. They pay a flat fee of about 8-12% on each advance, repaid from Steam payouts.
problem: Valve pays about 30 days after month-end, so a launch-week spike reaches the bank up to two months later. In that gap the studio sees ads producing wishlists at a profit (say $1-2 per wishlist, with 15-25% converting to first-week sales) but has no cash to scale the spend, pay for a console port or fund localization. Indie Fund and new funds like Blue Ocean's $30M (2026) back development, not post-launch receivables. Banks treat games as hit-driven lotteries.
solution: A 'Payout Bridge'. The studio connects a read-only Steamworks financial and wishlist key. We forecast net receipts for the next 60-90 days from launch-day wishlists, demo conversion, regional mix and refund rate. We advance 30-50% of that forecast, or pay ad platforms and streamers directly as an 'ad float'. The studio points its Steam payout to a sweep account so repayment comes off the top. A free 'Steam funnel benchmark' dashboard built on the same keys is the top of the funnel and the data moat.
why_now: Steam gets roughly 20k releases a year, so marketing spend, not development, is now the main cost and the main cash-flow gap. Small funds are proving capital appetite for indies in 2026. Steam Machine (June 2026) and Steam Frame (Sept 2026) are widening the PC base. LLM tooling makes per-game underwriting cheap enough for $10-40k tickets.
revenue_model: A flat 8-12% fee on each advance, 60-120 day terms, with a fee premium for the ad-float product. Later: a subscription for the benchmark dashboard, and a securitized pool sold to a credit fund.
non_obvious_insight: A lender doesn't need the right tail that VCs obsess over. The first 30 days of Steam sales track launch-day wishlists within a fairly tight band, and Valve is a reliable payer. So credit risk is behavioural (the studio changing its bank details) and can be solved with a sweep account, not with taste in games. Underwrite the wishlist funnel and ignore game quality.
first_30_days: Ship the free Steamworks-key benchmark dashboard and seed it in Steam dev Discords, r/gamedev and the wishlist-marketing newsletters. Raise a $150-250k first-loss pool from angels or a small credit line. Manually underwrite 5-10 advances of $10-40k for studios that just launched or have a Next Fest spike. Get a fintech lawyer to structure it as a purchase of receivables.

title: Burn Boss: Prescribed Fire as a Service
one_liner: AI burn-window planning, permits, drone ignition crews and liability cover, so landowners can safely burn and insurers can pay for the risk reduction.
customer: Private landowners, ranchers, timber owners, prescribed burn associations, water districts and utilities in TX, OK, OR, CA and CO. Insurers and reinsurers later pay for outcomes.
problem: Prescribed fire is the most effective fuel-reduction tool and the least scaled. Barriers are burn-plan expertise, weather windows, permits and smoke filings, liability insurance and crew logistics, not the fire itself.
solution: Start with a burn-plan generator and weather-window alerts built on AI forecast ensembles, plus a permit and smoke-filing packet, sold to burn associations. Then add a drone-ignition operator network and a liability wrap through a partner MGA. Add verified before/after fuel maps that insurers can underwrite (check state burn-liability rules).
why_now: AI weather models became operational in 2025 (such as ECMWF's AIFS), drone aerial ignition has matured, and record reinsurance capital wants provable mitigation. Several states have been reforming burn liability law (verify).
revenue_model: $1-3K per burn plan, per-acre service fees, and later outcome payments from carriers or utilities.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is planning and liability, not fire. Insurers can pay because treated acreage lowers their probable maximum loss.
first_30_days: Join 3 burn associations, ship window alerts and the plan generator, and run 5 paid burns.

title: Contractor Location and Payout Attestation for Sanctions Safety
one_liner: Continuous proof that remote contractors are where they say and are paid where they claim, giving employers evidence against North Korean IT-worker sanctions exposure.
customer: Startups and mid-market engineering-heavy firms using contractors, EOR and payroll platforms, staffing firms, and cyber-insurance brokers as a channel.
problem: North Korean IT-worker schemes hit 'nearly 70' and 'over 100' US companies in cases sentenced in April and May 2026. Deepfaked interviews and rented identities pass document checks, and laptops go to US-based farms. Paying a sanctioned actor is strict liability under OFAC, so the real fear for a CFO is not a fake candidate but a sanctions violation and forfeiture.
solution: Three layers: (1) a light first-90-day attestation (IP and VPN patterns, remote-access and KVM-over-IP detection, device continuity with the interview session); (2) payout-account screening (third-party or country mismatches, many workers to one account, crypto payouts); (3) shipping-address risk scoring. Output is an evidence file counsel can hand to a regulator or insurer.
why_now: The April and May 2026 sentencings show enforcement is real. Deepfake interviews are cheap and passing. The layer above hiring (payments and audit evidence) has no product, because hiring-fraud vendors focus on faces.
revenue_model: $15-30 per contractor per month, audit packs at $2-10K, insurer and broker referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The budget belongs to finance and legal, not HR or security, and the deliverable is evidence for regulators, not a risk score. Payout accounts are the chokepoint and are far easier to screen than faces.
first_30_days: Offer 20 startups a free payout-and-shipping exposure audit from a CSV export via VC platform teams and fractional-CFO networks. Convert to $500/month monitoring and sign one cyber-insurance broker.

title: Publish the Obvious: Generative Prior Art vs. Patent Thickets
one_liner: Turn cheap AI generation into a defensive weapon by industrially publishing dated, enabling disclosures of every obvious variant around a product, so secondary 'evergreening' and troll patents can't be granted.
customer: Primary: generic and biosimilar manufacturers and public-interest funders (procurement agencies, health-access NGOs) facing secondary patent thickets on drugs losing primary protection. Secondary: hardware, robotics and protocol-foundation startups afraid of patent trolls.
problem: Secondary patents on dosing regimens, polymorphs, formulations, devices and manufacturing tweaks extend monopolies long after the core compound expires, and they are cheap to file, especially now that AI drafts applications. Challengers' tools (IPR, oppositions, litigation) are expensive and come after the patent issues. Startups have no defense budget against troll assertions.
solution: A pipeline in which LLMs plus a patent agent or PhD reviewer enumerate the design space around a target product: formulations, dose schedules, salt and crystal forms, delivery devices, process variations. It drafts enabling defensive disclosures and timestamps them. It deposits them where examiners actually search (IP.com Prior Art Database, Research Disclosure, plus DOI-bearing repositories such as Zenodo and ChemRxiv that patent-office non-patent-literature tools crawl). It then monitors new filings, maps which disclosures block which claims, and files third-party submissions where the law allows. Sold as a per-product 'novelty shield' with measurable outcomes: examiner citations and rejections.
why_now: Compound patents on semaglutide and other blockbuster GLP-1s are expiring in several large markets in 2026, triggering a stampede of generic entry and follow-on patent strategies. LLMs now make it cheap to enumerate enabling variants at scale. Patent offices are swamped and revising guidance on AI-assisted work, and nobody has industrialized the defensive side of the novelty game.
revenue_model: $15-80k per product-family shield for generics and funders; $500-2k/month subscriptions for startups and foundations; success-based bonuses when a filing is rejected citing a disclosure; grant and NGO funding for public-health targets.
non_obvious_insight: Prior-art status depends on what was publicly and enablingly disclosed, not on who or what wrote it. So when generating variations is free, the asymmetric weapon is to publish the space before anyone can claim it. The scarce thing is no longer ideas but credible, discoverable, dated publication. It also aligns the incentive: the parties who pay (generics, health funders) gain directly from the commons staying open.
first_30_days: Pick 3 products with visible secondary-patent thickets and imminent generic entry. Produce about 200 enabling disclosures per product, each reviewed by a contracted patent agent. Publish to two or three searchable indexes. Send free 'thicket map' reports to 5 generic makers and 2 access-focused funders. Sell the first shield for $15-25k. Track later filings to prove examiner citations. Have patent counsel vet the approach up front, including that every disclosure is actually enabling and accurate.

title: Proof-of-Review Receipts for AI-Using Professionals
one_liner: A tamper-evident record that a named, licensed human actually reviewed AI output, backed by planted-error vigilance tests, sold to firms and their malpractice carriers.
customer: Mid-size law firms, accounting firms and physician groups using AI drafting or scribes, and the malpractice and E&O carriers, MGAs and brokers underwriting AI use.
problem: Courts worldwide have issued about 1,490 decisions on AI-hallucinated filings (1,000+ in the US by May 2026), with sanctions up to $110k and the first suspensions. More than 60% of carriers now ask about AI use in underwriting, and some add AI endorsements or exclusions. Firms cannot prove that attorney review happened beyond a policy memo.
solution: A review layer (Word and Outlook add-in, EHR plug-in, browser extension) that logs what the AI produced, what the human changed, dwell time, automated cite-check results and sign-off. It also seeds a random slice of reviews with canary errors (a fake citation, a wrong dose in a test document) to measure whether reviewers really catch them. A signed monthly review-integrity report goes to the carrier for premium credit or endorsement eligibility.
why_now: AI-hallucination sanctions are growing by about eight cases a day. The EPIC 2026 claims survey shows carriers seeing more AI-related claims, and carriers are rewriting applications and endorsements now.
revenue_model: $30-80 per professional per month, carrier and broker partnerships (revenue share on premium credits), and a cite-check add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The weak link is automation complacency, not just model hallucination. You can measure complacency the way airports measure screener vigilance, by planting known-bad items. Insurers will pay for measured human vigilance because it is a rating factor.
first_30_days: Partner with one legal-malpractice MGA or broker and 10 small firms (5-50 lawyers) through state-bar CLE channels. Ship a Word add-in that logs review and checks citations. Pilot canary errors with written consent.

title: Reverse-Angi: Shops Sell Their Overflow Jobs
one_liner: Missed calls and too-busy jobs get routed to a trusted peer shop that pays the originating shop a referral fee.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and handyman shops with 1-15 techs in one metro, organized in trade circles that already vouch for each other.
problem: About 48% of home-services calls never reach a person (Invoca). Homeowners cite too-busy (21%) and no-response (14%) as barriers to hiring. Angi charges $15-85 per lead that is shared with many bidders, so shops distrust lead-gen. AI receptionists are crowded and merely take messages a shop cannot service.
solution: Shops forward busy, after-hours or out-of-scope calls to a number that answers in seconds, qualifies the job and offers it to the best-matched peer with capacity today. The job is transferred as an exclusive, pre-qualified lead. The originating shop earns a referral share of the invoice and the receiving shop pays a platform fee. Trust comes from peer vouching and network ratings. Cross-trade referrals (plumber to HVAC to electrician) are included.
why_now: In a labor-short market capacity is scarcer than demand: 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects. Lead-gen distrust is high and ServiceTitan is moving upmarket. Real-time voice AI now handles triage well enough to answer instantly.
revenue_model: 20% of transferred-job revenue paid by the receiving shop, split about 10% to the originating shop and 10% to the platform. No subscription, so no adoption friction.
non_obvious_insight: In a labor-short market leads are not scarce, capacity is. Every busy shop is currently throwing away leads, so turn each shop from a lead buyer into a lead seller. It inverts Angi's economics: shops earn money for the calls they cannot take.
first_30_days: Seed 25 shops in one metro through local association groups. Use a Twilio number and a human dispatcher first. Settle via ACH. Track transfers and conversions weekly.

title: Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion
one_liner: A completion contractor that takes half-built solar jobs abandoned by bankrupt installers all the way to permission-to-operate, and is paid by the lenders whose loans go bad while the system sits dark.
customer: Solar loan originators and servicers, and TPO sponsors, that now hold stranded projects. The seven finance partners named in the Freedom Forever order are the first buyers: GoodLeap, EnFin, Credit Human, EverBright, Participate, Project Solar and Sunrun. Credit unions and ABS trustees holding 2023-2025 solar loans are the second wave. Homeowners are the beneficiary but do not pay.
problem: When a big installer dies, thousands of systems are left installed but not energized, or half-built. Freedom Forever went Chapter 11 in April 2026 and converted to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026, with about 1,600 layoffs. The borrower stops paying a $30-50k loan on a roof that produces nothing. Lender, homeowner and dead installer each say it is someone else's job. The court let lenders hire new contractors and push systems to PTO, but a lender has no bench of crews and no playbook for doing it.
solution: Run the work as a records-recovery business first and a crew business second. For each stranded job, build a forensic pack: the AHJ permit file, the utility interconnection record, the design set from the dead company's design and CRM tools, equipment serials from distributors and consignment records, and a site photo audit. Sort jobs into tiers: paperwork-only (contractor of record and engineer's stamp need re-issuing), inspection fix, missing hardware, and never started (unwind and refund path). Price each tier at a fixed fee plus a bonus at PTO, and subcontract the labor to licensed local electricians and laid-off installer crews. Give the lender a dashboard of its whole stranded book with cost to cure and expected PTO date.
why_now: Freedom Forever's Chapter 7 conversion (Aug 2026, creditor claims due Oct 16, 2026) and the court order letting financiers step in make this concrete now. Sunnova (June 2025), SunPower (Aug 2024) and 100+ other solar failures came before it. Post-25D volume is down in 2026, so more failures are likely. Lenders have step-in rights but no operating capacity.
revenue_model: Fixed completion fee of $1.5-4k per job by tier, plus a $500 success bonus at PTO, paid by the lender or servicer. Add a monthly stranded-book dashboard subscription. Later, sell a 12-month workmanship warranty on completed jobs, paid by the lender, and a retainer for standby capacity when the next installer fails.
non_obvious_insight: A stranded job is 80% a records and legal-standing problem, not a labor problem. Permits, interconnection applications, engineer stamps and design files sit in a dead contractor's name and portal logins, so nobody can legally finish even though laid-off crews are cheap and plentiful. Also, the buyer is the lender and not the homeowner. The lender's collateral is worthless while the system is dark, it already has contractual step-in rights, and outsiders assume the homeowner is the customer.
first_30_days: Message loss-mitigation and installer-failure leads at 3-4 lenders. Use former installer ops people on LinkedIn to get the introductions. Offer to complete 10 stranded jobs in one metro at cost-plus, with payment on PTO. Recruit 3 laid-off project managers or permit coordinators and 1-2 licensed electrician subs. Write the per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer checklist. Target the first 10 PTOs inside 60 days, with case studies from them.

title: Medicaid Work-Rule Retention Packets for Health Plans
one_liner: A pay-per-retained-member service that assembles the income-proxy, exemption and medical-frailty evidence packets Medicaid expansion enrollees need to keep coverage, sold to the health plans and clinics that lose revenue when members are dropped.
customer: Medicaid managed-care plans (especially regional and provider-sponsored plans in expansion states), FQHC networks, and hospital systems with large expansion panels. Secondary buyers: state agencies and counties that have said they will not add staff.
problem: Work requirements start January 1, 2027 in 44 states. CMS projects 2.3M people lose Medicaid in 2027, and 55% of enrollees are unaware of the rule. States are scraping existing data. Nebraska hired no new staff, and its medical-frailty code list omitted certain cancers, heart failure and HIV. North Carolina bars self-attestation and requires 3 months of records. About 25% of Dare County's expansion enrollees are self-employed. County Medicaid units have ~10% vacancy and staff with only 11-13 months' experience. A KFF-cited expert calls hours tracking 'a problem no state has solved at scale.'
solution: Consent-based enrollee flow, started via text or QR code at a clinic or from a plan's outreach. The enrollee links bank, gig-platform, payroll or 1099 data through open-banking and income-verification connectors. The system computes monthly income against the $580 threshold (80 hours x $7.25) that satisfies the rule, with seasonal averaging where the state allows. It then generates a state-formatted verification submission. In parallel it mines the plan's or clinic's claims and EHR history to match the medically frail categories and produces clinician attestation forms. It tracks the 30-day grace window and 6-month redeterminations. Volunteer-hour and school verification come from partner organizations. A human navigator queue handles exceptions.
why_now: CMS issued its interim final rule June 1, 2026 and a medical-frailty implementation deck on September 8. Nebraska (May 1) and Montana (July 1) are live, so real failure modes are visible. States may request extra information from enrollees in year one, and exemption self-attestation is allowed only once before 2028, so documentation becomes mandatory after that. The January deadline sets hard budget urgency.
revenue_model: Per-packet fee plus per-member-per-month retention fee paid by the plan or clinic. Assumption to validate: a retained expansion member is worth hundreds of dollars per month in capitation, so $30-100 per retained member is easily justified. Optional state contracts priced per verification.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is evidence for people the state cannot see in wage data (self-employed, gig, seasonal), not caseworker capacity. Health plans and clinics, not states, have both the financial incentive and the claims data to prove frailty. The federal income equivalent ($580/month) turns an impossible hours-tracking problem into a cash-flow calculation. Evidence: NC counties describe the informal-economy documentation gap, 10% vacancy, no self-attestation and 3 months of records (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Nebraska confirmed the ~$580 income option and said it will not hire or add staff (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-closer-look-at-nebraska-the-first-state-planning-to-implement-a-medicaid-work-requirement/), and its frailty code list had gaps (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/nebraska-medicaid-work-requirements-launch-first-state/818992/). CMS projects 2.3M coverage losses in 2027 (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/cms-medicaid-work-requirements-final-rule-state-guidance/821631/). State staffing gaps: https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/. Risk: 26 states are suing over the rule.
first_30_days: Offer free pilots to 1-2 FQHCs in Nebraska or Montana, where enrollees already face the requirement. Build on an open-banking connector and an income-verification API. Draft the income-proxy calculator and a frailty-evidence template from CMS's September deck. Book meetings with member-retention leads at 5 regional Medicaid plans, with a paid pilot targeted for the November-December pre-January enrollment wave. Get a HIPAA BAA and consent language in place first.

title: Cooler-Door Pivot for THC Beverage Brands
one_liner: A 45-day pivot studio that moves hemp-THC drink and gummy brands into compliant functional products under their existing distributor and retailer slots, plus a per-container THC ledger for distributors and retailers.
customer: Small and mid-size hemp-THC beverage and edible brands, beverage distributors including alcohol-licensed ones, and convenience, liquor and smoke-shop chains holding hemp SKUs. Brands pay for the pivot sprint and co-pack. Distributors and retailers pay a subscription for the SKU ledger.
problem: P.L. 119-37 redefines hemp to 0.4 mg total THC per container. The effective date was pushed from Nov 12 to Dec 11, 2026 by H.R. 6500 (signed Sept 2), while synthetic cannabinoids lose hemp status on Nov 12. The US Hemp Roundtable estimates about 95% of existing products fall outside the new definition, and a typical THC drink has 2-10 mg per can. There is no federal sell-through safe harbor. The industry employs about 350,000 people. Distributors are asking whether alcohol-licensed wholesalers can even accept returns in three-tier states, and operators face a liquidity problem, not a compliance problem.
solution: Two parts. First, an SKU ledger where COAs and pack volumes are converted into per-container total THC (delta-9 plus decarboxylated THCA) and a keep, pull or return status by state, with vendor chargeback letters and a documented disposition trail. Second, a pivot studio that reuses the brand's flavor systems, cans and design to launch adaptogen, functional or non-alcoholic SKUs through a vetted co-packer, so the brand keeps its distributor agreements and planogram slots. An optional bridge licenses the brand to a state-licensed cannabis producer, since licensed dispensaries are unaffected by the federal redefinition.
why_now: The reprieve to Dec 11 gives roughly 10 weeks. Four congressional frameworks are pending: Barr, Van Duyne and Landsman, Comer, and a Sheehy-Klobuchar Senate companion. The ledger works whether Congress bans or regulates, because age-21, testing and labeling regimes would still need lab-verified per-container data. Retailers and distributors are already telling counsel to audit inventory and plan wind-downs, and gummy prices are reported at 30-50% of 2025 levels.
revenue_model: $5-15k fixed fee per brand pivot sprint, plus a 2-5% royalty or co-pack margin on the pivot SKUs. $199-499 per month per distributor or retail chain for the SKU ledger and chargeback tooling. Finder fee on brand-licensing deals to licensed operators.
non_obvious_insight: As Harris Sliwoski puts it, 'The problem for many operators will not be compliance but liquidity' (https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/what-the-2026-federal-hemp-ban-means-for-unsold-hemp-inventory/). The scarce asset of a THC-drink brand is not inventory, which is illiquid and repricing downward, but its cooler-door slots and distributor agreements, which are among the hardest things to win in beverages. Those slots vanish if the brand disappears. The per-container standard turns an impossible reformulation into a category switch: LearnBrands notes the demand is being inherited by non-alcoholic beer, alcohol-removed wine and functional beverages (https://www.learnbrands.com/post/hemp-thc-beverage-ban-november-2026). Sources on the reprieve and stakes: https://foleyhoag.com/news-and-insights/blogs/cannabis-and-the-law/2026/september/a-temporary-reprieve-for-hemp-thc-products%E2%80%A6-but-what-now/ and https://www.ediblerank.com/legal/hemp-ban-timeline
first_30_days: Pull 40 THC-beverage brands from distributor and retailer press lists and offer a free exposure scan built from their COAs and volumes. Sell three paid pivot sprints. Line up one co-packer with non-alcoholic and adaptogen capability. Pilot the SKU ledger with two distributors and one c-store chain, producing their pull and return list.

title: Universal Insurance Claims Rails for Vet Front Desks
one_liner: Vet front desks lose hours filing claims in a dozen insurer portals; sell them one submission and status layer, then add pre-approval and instant-pay as insurers plug in.
customer: Independent clinics and small groups (1-20 locations) with 15-30% insured patients. Later, insurers as per-claim payers.
problem: There are about 6.98M insured animals (+9% in 2025), each insurer has its own portal, forms and record requests, and only 48.2% of practices proactively recommend insurance. Owners often front the full bill. Insurers cannot see clinics, so they lack pre-authorization, real-time pricing and fraud tools.
solution: A browser agent inside the PIMS invoice screen, later API-connected, sends invoice plus records to the right insurer by policy number, tracks status, chases missing documents and reconciles payments. Once volume gives risk data, offer a direct-pay advance so the owner only pays the deductible at checkout.
why_now: Insured animals keep growing while premiums outpace enrollment, so insurers want lower cost-to-adjudicate. Computer-use LLM agents can operate portals without waiting for API deals. Ambient scribes are producing more structured records for claims.
revenue_model: $99-199 per clinic per month, $1-3 per clean claim from insurers later, and a 2-3% fee on advanced claims.
non_obvious_insight: Insurance penetration is partly a back-office problem: the clinic is the distribution channel and is punished with admin work for recommending coverage. Remove the penalty and the recommendation rate rises. The clearinghouse owns the claims data insurers currently cannot see.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 clinics through cloud-PIMS user groups. Shadow the front desk for a week and automate the top 5 insurers by portal. Offer 30 days free, then $99 per month. Measure hours saved per week and days-to-payment.

title: Groundskeepers: Custodianship for AI-Built Software
one_liner: Property management for software: a monthly subscription where a named junior-developer 'groundskeeper' keeps small businesses' AI-built apps patched, backed up, monitored, and alive, with a senior signing off.
customer: SMBs (multi-location dentists, HVAC firms, property managers, boutique agencies) and solo founders who built internal tools or products with Lovable, Replit, Cursor and similar. $149-499/month per app. Agencies that built apps for clients can white-label.
problem: Building is free but owning is not. 'Vibe-code cleanup' is a recognized freelance niche, but it is a one-time project. After the rescue no one is responsible for dependency updates, key rotation, backups, uptime, model deprecations, and API changes, and a large share of production vibe-coded apps hit an incident within 90 days.
solution: A fixed-price move-in inspection ($900), then a monthly custody plan with monitoring, patching, backup verification, a lightweight quarterly security check, a runbook, and one accountable human with an incident SLA. Groundskeepers are laid-off junior developers, each managing 25-40 apps on a standardized template stack with AI tooling, supervised by fractional seniors. The plan includes an 'exit ramp' to rebuild or retire the app.
why_now: In 2026 a flood of AI-built apps entered production and cleanup specialists are one of the fastest-growing freelance niches, per Forbes coverage. Junior developer hiring has dried up, so skilled, cheap talent is abundant. Cyber insurers are beginning to care about managed versus unmanaged apps.
revenue_model: Recurring subscription, inspection fees, incident retainers, exit-ramp rebuilds, and referral fees from cyber insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The market frames this as cleanup (a project) but the durable business is custody (a relationship), like property management versus house flipping. The same structure gives displaced juniors a career ladder: custody is the residency that produces the senior engineers the industry stopped training.
first_30_days: Offer free move-in inspections to the first 20 apps through Lovable and Replit communities, local chambers of commerce, and SMB Facebook groups. Hire 2 laid-off juniors. Assemble monitoring from off-the-shelf tools (Sentry, uptime checks, Dependabot). Target 15 paying customers at about $199, roughly $3k monthly recurring revenue, by day 90.

title: Vacant Inherited-Home Insurance and Caretaking
one_liner: A bundled insurance-plus-sensors-plus-caretaker program for the house that sits empty during probate.
customer: Executors and heirs of a decedent's home, reached through probate attorneys, funeral homes and hospice social workers. Insurers and MGAs are the capacity partners.
problem: Homeowners policies typically restrict coverage for vandalism, freezing and other perils once a home is vacant 30-60 days, which is exactly when no probate court has appointed anyone. Probate often takes 9-18 months (unverified estimate). A burst pipe or break-in lands on an amateur executor, who may be personally exposed. Property taxes and utilities also keep running.
solution: An MGA-backed 'Estate Home Program' with a vacant-dwelling policy placed with a surplus-lines carrier, water and temperature sensors, weekly visits, lock rekeying and mail handling, utility transfer to the executor, and an optional executor advance for carrying costs repaid at sale. Add clean-out and sale-prep referrals.
why_now: Housing wealth is starting to flow from Boomers. Insurers tightened property underwriting after recent nonrenewal waves, and cheap IoT sensors make monitoring practical.
revenue_model: MGA commission (10-20%), a $150-$300/month program fee, and margin on clean-out and sale-prep referrals.
non_obvious_insight: The house effectively becomes uninsurable at the exact moment the owner dies, and nobody owns that timing gap. Executors find out after the loss.
first_30_days: Find an E&S broker who writes vacant dwellings and design a 'vacant estate' placement. Sign 5 probate attorneys and test with 10 houses. Confirm state vacancy and insurable-interest rules with a licensed agent.

title: Member-Owned Healthspan Co-ops on the HSA Cap
one_liner: Affinity groups of 300-400 households co-own a small primary-care practice on a roughly $99-129 monthly membership that is now HSA-compatible, use group visits, and buy elite screening at pooled cash prices.
customer: Self-employed and small-business households aged 40-64 on bronze, catastrophic or high-deductible plans who already belong to a trusted group: a congregation, a 55+ community, a chamber of commerce or freelancers' guild, a farmers-market vendors' association, a large local gym.
problem: Elite prevention is sold item by item at retail prices ($200-$2,500 per test), by clinics whose upsell incentives people distrust. Direct primary care exists but rarely includes a preventive protocol and does not pool purchasing power. High deductibles leave the middle class with either a rushed annual physical or nothing between that and an emergency.
solution: A consumer co-op that hires one physician, one NP or health coach and part-time admin on a fixed monthly fee under the direct-primary-care rules. Monthly group visits (60-90 minutes, about 12 members each) cover a rotating theme (blood pressure, lipids and ApoB, sleep, strength, metabolic health) with each member's numbers on a private dashboard, plus 1:1 visits, messaging and same-week appointments. The co-op negotiates cash prices for in-office and send-out labs, coronary calcium scans, DEXA and VO2 testing (paid separately as ordinary HSA-eligible medical expenses), and members vote on which tests the protocol includes, so there is no upsell incentive. The startup provides the co-op in a box: legal templates, protocol, software, physician recruiting and a shared purchasing agreement.
why_now: Since January 1, 2026, direct primary care fees of up to $150 per month for an individual ($300 for a family) no longer disqualify someone from an HSA, and bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans became HSA-eligible, opening HSAs to roughly 7.3 million more Americans. That creates a tax-advantaged price point for exactly this product. DPC statutes exist in most states, and cash-price transparency for imaging and labs is improving.
revenue_model: Members pay the co-op $99-129 per month; the startup earns a platform and management fee of about 12-15% (roughly $15-20 per member per month) plus a $10-15k organizing fee per launch. Group purchasing agreements are structured as flat fees to stay clear of anti-kickback problems.
non_obvious_insight: The HSA rule sets a $150 ceiling that is roughly enough to fund a physician and coach if 400 households pool their membership, and the cooperative form solves the two things that block middle-class longevity medicine: trust (members own the practice and vote on the protocol) and price (pooled buying power). Group visits will not improve outcomes by themselves, as the evidence shows they are roughly equivalent to usual care, but they stretch physician time across more patients. Affinity groups already hold the trust and distribution; one founding meeting is the sales cycle.
first_30_days: Pair a burned-out primary-care physician or existing DPC doctor with one affinity group (a 400-member gym or 55+ community works). Hold a 60-minute founding meeting and collect pledge cards for 150 founding members at $99 per month. Get a state-specific legal and HSA-compliance memo on DPC and cooperative structure. Line up wholesale lab accounts and cash-price quotes from two imaging centers. Open in shared space with the first cohort within about 3-4 months.
